title: The sea (Exodus 14:10–31)
hook: the sea ahead, chariots behind: stand still and see

segments.voice: Yesterday, out in haste: dough carried on shoulders, a mixed multitude, a night to be remembered. Your line was unleavened, in a hurry. What did you let go out the door unfinished? Day three hundred eighty-eight.

They're free for a few days, and then Pharaoh changes his mind one last time. Why did we let our slaves go? He takes six hundred chosen chariots and all the chariots of Egypt and chases them. The Israelites are camped by the sea. They look up and see the dust cloud coming. Water in front of them. Army behind them. No way around. And the people turn on Moses with one of the bitterest lines in the Bible, in the King James translation: "Because there were no graves in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness?" We told you to leave us alone. Slavery was better than this.
screen: `PHARAOH CHANGES HIS MIND.` → `SEA AHEAD, CHARIOTS BEHIND.` → `NO GRAVES IN EGYPT?`

segments.voice: Moses answers: "Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will shew to you to day." And then: "The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace." Stand still. Be quiet. Watch. When you're terrified, that's the hardest instruction there is. And then, strangely, God says almost the opposite: "Wherefore criest thou unto me? speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward." Stand still, and go forward. Both. The stillness isn't doing nothing. It's stopping the panic, so you can see the way when it opens. Moses stretches out his hand. A strong east wind blows all night and drives the sea back. And the people walk through on dry ground, "and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left." The Egyptians follow, the wheels of their chariots clog, the water returns, and the army is lost. The Hebrew name for this water is yam suph. It's often translated Red Sea, but suph usually means reeds, so many scholars say Sea of Reeds, and nobody knows for sure where it was. A later Jewish story tells of a man named Nahshon who walked into the water up to his neck before it parted. Christians have read this crossing as a picture of baptism: Paul writes that the Israelites were baptized in the cloud and in the sea. That's why Exodus fourteen is read at the Easter Vigil in Catholic and many other churches, the night new Christians are baptized. Through the water, from slavery to freedom.
screen: `FEAR YE NOT. STAND STILL.` · `SPEAK, THAT THEY GO FORWARD.` · `A WALL ON THE RIGHT AND LEFT.` · `YAM SUPH: SEA OF REEDS.` · then, large: `STAND STILL, AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand still for one minute. If you can, stand up. Feet flat, arms loose, eyes open or closed. Think of the thing that feels like chariots behind you right now, the worry that's chasing you. Don't run from it, and don't fight it. Just stand still. Let your breathing slow. Notice that you are here, and you are standing. If you pray, you can say Moses's words: fear not, stand still. If you don't, just stay still, and see what you notice. The bell holds the time.
The sea. The water Israel crossed on dry ground, with an army behind and a wall of water on either side.
Your line: stand still and see. Today, before you react to the next thing that panics you, stand still for three breaths, then take one step forward. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Exodus 14 is read at the Easter Vigil in Catholic and many other churches, linking the crossing of the sea to baptism, and Christians often turn to "stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD" in times of fear.

fork.setup: you're Moses. sea in front, chariots behind, and your people saying they'd rather be slaves. what do you tell them?
options: run along the shore and scatter.
fear not, stand still, and see.
go back and surrender to Pharaoh.
fork.reveal: "Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD." then God says: tell them to go forward. stillness first, then the step.

original.note: Hebrew: the sea of reeds, traditionally translated Red Sea.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses parted the Red Sea.
what it means: terrified people are told to stand still and see, then to go forward, through the water to freedom.
what a scholar hears: yam suph most likely means sea of reeds; the Greek translation gave us Red Sea, and the crossing's location is still debated.

notes: Nahshon story: Babylonian Talmud Sotah 37a (and Mekhilta); presented as 'a later Jewish story'. Confirm.
yam suph / Sea of Reeds and the Septuagint's 'Red Sea' (erythra thalassa). Confirm.
Easter Vigil: Exodus 14:15–15:1 is the one Old Testament reading that may not be omitted in the Roman Rite; 'Catholic and many other churches' should be confirmed for other traditions.
The Egyptians' deaths are stated briefly; tomorrow's lesson includes a Jewish teaching about not rejoicing at enemies' deaths.
